fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes a generally ductile single-phase CrMnFeCoNi-type FCC alloy for the brittle dual-phase lamellar Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy.
It proposes severe plastic deformation and low-temperature annealing rather than the required 6 GPa, 1473 K, 2-hour HPHT treatment.
It omits the FCC/B2 lamellar-to-hierarchical transformation and coherent FCC/B2 interfaces central to the target mechanism.
The cited evidence does not establish that low-temperature annealing stabilizes SPD-induced nanotwins or produces simultaneous room-temperature strength and ductility gains in the proposed state.

The predicted elongation and fracture-toughness thresholds are extrapolated from evidence on unprocessed or cryogenically tested alloys rather than demonstrated for the proposed SPD-plus-annealing route.
explanation: This is a scientifically recognizable strength–ductility hypothesis based on ultrafine grains and coherent twin boundaries, but it is not a reconstruction of the target strategy. It changes the alloy class, initial microstructure, processing route, parameter regime, structural mediator, and deformation mechanism. The only substantive overlap is the general idea that coherent interfaces can both impede and transmit dislocations. Its control experiment can distinguish SPD plus annealing from annealing or SPD alone, but it cannot test the target distinction between HPHT and conventional lower-pressure thermal treatments. Evidence supports room-temperature twinning after high-pressure torsion and generic coherent-boundary strengthening, yet does not directly support annealing-mediated twin stabilization or the quantitative mechanical predictions. Accordingly, it is best classified as a plausible but weakly evidenced alternative.
